replying_to: Replying to Leveraging variational autoencoders for multiple data imputation
display_title: Official Review of Paper1070 by Reviewer 29B2

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper considers using variational autoencoders for imputation when data are missing at random when modeling large datasets (e.g. genomic observations). The paper weaves together several independently useful ideas into one coherent approach:

* Do multiple imputation (sample each missing value M times), rather than single imputation
* Use a power likelihood (raise to 1/\beta, for \beta > 1) to be robust to model misspecification

The presented approach can be achieved via 3 different ways to sample missingness: pseudo-Gibbs (PG, Sec. 3.1.1), metropolis-within-Gibbs (MWG, Sec. 3.1.2), or sampling importance-resampling (SIR, Sec. 3.1.3). 

The method is applied within a *cross validation* framework where artificial MCAR missingness is added to each fold, then the imputation abilities of various settings of hyperparameter \beta (and other factors like number of epochs, learning rate) are assessed using a mean absolute error (MAE) performance metric across folds and an optimal value is chosen.

Evaluations consider a large genomics dataset: 17,000 features representing each of 667 cancer patients; each patient can be labeled by a cancer type (either GBM or LGG). Experiments introduce artificial missingness, and then try to compare methods in terms of the ability to estimate these missing values in terms of MAE, or the ability to predict the cancer type given observed values, in terms of either predictive accuracy (MAE) or in ability to identify relevant features (false discovery rate).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

* Multiple rather than single imputation is of interest
* Use of power likelihood to be robust to misspecification is useful
* Demonstration of coverage only with \beta > 1 (Fig 1 to Fig 2) is compelling
* Plots of imputed values in rank order (Fig 1-2) nicely demonstrate that imputed values in the tails are biased toward the mean
* Story about reduced false discovery rates for multiple imputation in Table 1 is compelling

# Weaknesses

Here I list the primary weaknesses as I see them (each is elaborated below under its respective heading of Quality/Clarity/Reproducibility)

* W1: Evaluation limited to only one dataset (though it is an interesting one)
* W2: Focus on MAE evaluation metric, but do not use absolute error to inspire the imputation estimator
* W3: Focus on limited setting (Missing at random), though MNAR more realistic
* W4: Reproducibility difficult: Network architecture and other design choices not available
* W5: Little difference between imputation methods (PG, MWG, SIR)

To me, W1 and W4 are the biggest issues that prevent recommending acceptance.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Novelty

The work builds heavily on the genomic-focused imputation work of Qiu et al (2020). 
That work does single imputation with \beta VAEs, while this present work is focused on multiple imputation.

This work makes a nice connection between \beta VAEs and the power likelihood (Bissiri et al 2016, Holmes & Walker 2017)
I'll note this connection has already been published, see Theorem 2 of Camuto et al. 2021 (http://proceedings.mlr.press/v130/camuto21a/camuto21a.pdf)

Additionally, the key sampling steps used here are all inspired by previous work, including:
* PG from Rezende et al. 2014
* MWG from Mattei & Frellsen (2018)
* SIR from Mattei & Frellsen (2019)

The adaptation of each of these to the power likelihood approach is straightforward (just raise likelihood to 1/\beta).

Thus, the key claims to innovation here as I see them are:
* realizing the straightforward use of multiple imputations with a power-likelihood VAE
* using cross-validation with artificial missingness to select \beta

To my eye, these all seem valuable though are straightforward extensions of prior work. I rate the technical novelty here as modest.

## Quality

I see the 3 issues below (W1-W3) as all limiting the potential impact and significance of these findings

### W1: Evaluation limited to only one dataset (though it is an interesting one)

Without more datasets, the claims here are difficult to justify as holding generally. 
Even on the dataset in question, a few facts need to be added, such as:
* does it have any true missingness? (before the artificial missingness of this approach is applied)
* if so, what missingness paradigm (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) is most suitable to describe the reason for the missingness?
* are all features continuous, unconstrained real values? e.g. why is the Gaussianity assumption appropriate?

I'd suggest at least 2 other datasets are needed, though I know this is a lot of work to ask. Perhaps with each other dataset, only one of PG/MWG/SIR routines would be used.


### W2: Focus on MAE evaluation metric, but do not use absolute error to inspire the imputation estimator

In Sec 2.2, the paper explains that estimating the *mean* of the posterior over x_mis given x_obs is motivated because it is the estimator because it minimizes *squared error* loss.

The focus in all evaluations, however, is the mean *absolute error* (MAE), for which it is well-known that the posterior **median** is the best estimator.

For simple Gaussians, of course, the median is the mean, but I am wondering if the authors can comment about whether when using more complex distributions (e.g. sampling from the joint over x_mis and z as in PG) and making approximations of q instead of the real posterior over latent variables, if using the median over M samples (rather than the mean) would yield better scores on the MAE metric.


### W3: Focus on limited setting (Missing at random), though MNAR more realistic

While simpler settings like MCAR and MAR are often difficult enough, I'll just flag that a major limitation of this method is that it cannot apply to missing not-at-random data. I'm no domain expert at the particular genomic analysis pursued in this paper, so I'd be happy to acknowledge that MNAR isn't applicable there if the authors argue convincingly, but in my experience almost any biomedical data with missing entries almost always is best modeled by MNAR assumptions.




## Clarity / Reproducibility

Overall the manuscript got its main points across to me without difficulty.

However, I would not be able to reproduce at present, due to issue W4 below.
The supplement *promises* to release code, which is a good start, but not enough... many choices need to be explicitly documented at least in the supplement.

### W4: Network architecture and other design choices not available

Several key elements of the method are not in the manuscript, making reproducibility next to impossible from manuscript alone:

* specific architecture/sizes of the encoder and decoder of the VAE
* optimization method used (SGD? ADAM? adagrad?)
* batch size
* number of iterations of the PG/MWG routines

### W5: Little difference in practice between imputation methods (PG, MWG, SIR)

The paper goes a long way to present 3 distinct methods for sampling imputations.
However, in experiments it is difficult to see much difference between these (e.g. in Fig 2, the MAE of all 3 methods is within 0.05; in Tab. 1 the false discovery rate is the same for all 3 methods). 

As a matter of presentation, I'd suggest recapping in the results section why we might expect little difference between these methods (e.g. is this a sign the approximate posterior q is quite good? and thus the correction term that makes MWG more accurate than PG is rarely needed?)
content.summary_of_the_review:
To me, W1 and W4 are the biggest issues that prevent recommending acceptance: readers can't reproduce this and can't generalize conclusions beyond one dataset. If W1 and W4 were addressed satisfactorily with improved updates to the manuscript, and if other issues were at least thoughtfully commented upon or acknowledged, I could imagine raising my score.

Technical novelty is also limited, though I think this marriage of multiple imputation and the power likelihood, while straightforward, does seem rather useful.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Motivated by the poor imputation coverage of variational autoencoders (VAEs) causing under and overestimation in imputed values, the authors propose using \beta-VAEs as an alternative and highlight that in order to achieve calibrated imputation, \beta needs to be estimated via cross-validation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well written and the idea of introducing missingness to aid with the selection of beta during cross-validation is interesting (though under explored, see below).

The paper has several important weaknesses:
- imputation being the focus, the authors fail to discuss different types of missingness and how they can be addressed with the proposed methodology.
- introducing missing values as part of the cross-validation procedure seems a good idea, however, the details about how missingness is introduced are not provided. The reviewer has to assume that missingness is introduced completely at random.
- the experiments are underwhelming for two key reasons: i) missingness in sequence-based gene expression data is not MCAR (not even MAR), so the experiment is completely artificial, and ii) the downstream experiment is welcome, however, using LASSO to identify gene signatures is problematic because it tends to exclude correlated genes resulting in false negatives and there are several (easy) existing approaches to reduce the false discovery rate in LASSO models, which are not necessarily caused by the imputation strategy but can be addressed by estimating confidence/credible intervals for the coefficients of the LASSO model.

As a minor point, Figure 1c does a poor job at justifying that imputations are underestimated at more extreme values. The authors should consider a more quantitative approach, for instance, calculating coverage for quantiles (say deciles or quartiles) of the data values (like in Figure A.4, which is provided with a proper description in the main text).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written, clear and easy to follow. Novelty is virtually non-existent, which paired with a clear explanation of the experimental settings and model parameters make for potentially good reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors explore an important problem. The paper is for the most part an application paper (which is not necessarily an issue, however, justifiably with very little novelty), but with limited empirical evidence. Specifically, the authors only consider one dataset, one missingness mechanism and one downstream task.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper demonstrates that Multiple Imputation schemes based on Variational AutoEncoders (VAEs) provide poor empirical coverage, i.e., the fraction of times where the true unknown value falls within the 95% confidence interval of the multiply imputed values is too low. They propose to use $\beta-$VAE instead of Vanilla VAE and show that they achieve better empirical coverage with similar imputation accuracy. Finally, they show that  using $\beta-$VAE instead of vanilla VAE allow to obtain better False Discovery Rates on a gene selection problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**.  
- The idea of tuning hyper-parameters on a variety of metrics including empirical coverage is new.  
- It is interesting to compare the 3 sampling strategies (pseudo-gibbs, metropolis-within-gibbs, sampling importance resampling) for multiple imputation.

**Weaknesses**.  
- **Restrictive experimental evaluation**: The experiments are provided for only one dataset, with MCAR missing values for 20% of the samples and one level of missingness (10%) for these incomplete samples.  

- **Soundness of the comparison VAE/$\beta$-VAE on empirical coverage**: For the standard VAE, the hyper-parameters chosen are the ones from Qiu et al (2020). For the $\beta$-VAE, the hyper-parameters are tuned by cross-validation to optimise both the imputation accuracy and the empirical coverage. It may be that VAE could produce coverage equivalent to that of $\beta$-VAE if their hyper-parameters were also tuned for coverage. Given the experimental setting, it seems hasty to conclude that $\beta$-VAE are better than VAE in terms of coverage.  

- **Soundness of the False Discovery rate analysis**: the authors compare the FDR of the different imputation schemes (with a VAE or $\beta$-VAE?). The FDR is computed by taking as ground truth the features selected by the sparse logistic regression on the complete data. It seems to me that the solution on the complete data is not unique, and that these features can’t be taken as the ground truth, or even the desirable target. Moreover, in the case of multiple imputation, the FDR computed highly depends on the choice of inclusion probability. It is also possible that if the sparse LR had been run several times on the singly imputed dataset, it would have provided different sets of selected genes which depending on the choice of inclusion probability could give better FDR.

- **Some important unclear points**:
  - What is the combined measure of Mean Absolute Error and Coverage that used to choose the best hyper-parameters for $\beta$-VAE?  
  - Some experimental details are missing: notably train/test sizes, cross-validation details.  
  - How was the sparsity parameter tuned for the FDR experiments with various imputations?  
  - It is unclear to me what training data is used to train the VAE and $\beta$-VAE. I understand that only the complete training points (samples) are used to train the VAE. Is it the same setting used for the $\beta$-VAE? If not, the comparison between VAE and $\beta$-VAE would not be on an equal basis. A better explanation of how missing values are handled at training time for $\beta$-VAE would be necessary.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written.

The $\beta$-VAE as well as the different sampling techniques considered for imputation are not new. The novelty resides in the experimental evaluation of the coverage provided by the different combinations of VAE and sampling techniques.

I have concerns regarding the clarity/reproducibility. As detailed in the previous section, many experimental details are missing.

Vocabulary note: The LASSO refers to linear regression with $\ell-1$ penalty. Thus the model used in the paper is a sparse logistic regression $\ell-1$ penalty and not a LASSO.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the concerns about the soundness of the experiments, the restrictive setting in which they are conducted, as well as the lack of clarity/precision in the description of the experiments, do not allow me to be convinced by the conclusions of the paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Paper proposes a multiple imputation framework using $\beta$- variational autoencoders. The proposed framework has advantage over the variational autoencoders based imputation frameworks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The problem of missing data affects almost every domain and is an important issue. And as the paper mentions, multiple imputation is a principled approach to deal with the issue compared to a single imputation.

The proposes method uses $\beta$-VAEs for multiple imputation, which is shown to have better coverage and provide better results than the standard VAE based approach. However, I am not sure why the empirical evaluation does not contain any comparison with other existing multiple imputation methods, such as GAIN [1], MIDA [2], MICE [3], etc. Where [1] and [3] are not included in the related work either.

[1] Yoon, J., Jordon, J., & Schaar, M. (2018, July). Gain: Missing data imputation using generative adversarial nets. In International conference on machine learning (pp. 5689-5698). PMLR.
[2] Gondara, L., & Wang, K. (2018, June). Mida: Multiple imputation using denoising autoencoders. In Pacific-Asia conference on knowledge discovery and data mining (pp. 260-272). Springer, Cham.
[3] Stef Buuren and Karin Groothuis-Oudshoorn. mice: Multivariate imputation by chained equations in r. Journal of statistical software, 45(3), 2011.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Paper is clearly written and is easily understandable. Novelty is weak as it is an extension of VAEs to multiple imputation, a problem studied before, but this does not diminish the contribution.
content.summary_of_the_review: please see my detailed review, if authors can answer my questions regarding comparison choice, I am open to increasing my score.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
